'''''Freesia laxa''''', commonly known as '''flowering grass''',<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/167668/i-Freesia-laxa-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Freesia laxa'' | accessdate = 27 February 2018}}</ref> is a small [[species]] of [[corm]]ous [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Iridaceae, from eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya to northeastern South Africa.<ref name=WCSP_Fl/> It is grown in gardens as an [[ornamental plant]].

==Description==
''Freesia laxa'' grows from corms, reaching about {{convert|15|-|30|cm|in|abbr=on|0}} tall. The green leaves are arranged in a flat "fan" from which the flower stalk emerges. The flowers are flattened, about {{convert|2|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} across. Their colour varies considerably. The ground colour is red, white or pale blue. The bases of the lowest three [[tepals]] usually have a darker marking, which may be red or purple, although it is absent in the pure white form. The seeds are bright red.<ref name=Math87>{{Citation |last=Mathew |first=Brian |year=1987 |title=The Smaller Bulbs |location=London |publisher=B.T. Batsford |isbn=978-0-7134-4922-8 }}, p. 9</ref><ref name=Inne85>{{Citation |last=Innes |first=Clive |year=1985 |title=The World of Iridaceae |location=Ashington, UK |publisher=Holly Gate International |isbn=978-0-948236-01-3 }}, p. 18</ref>

It is native to the eastern side of southern Africa,<ref name=Math87/> from [[Kenya]] to [[South Africa]],<ref name=WCSP_Fl/> where it grows in somewhat moist conditions. It dies down to a corm in the winter, growing again at the end of spring and flowering in summer.<ref name=Math87/> In the wild, in the Southern Hemisphere, it flowers between October and December.<ref name=Inne85/>

==Systematics==
This small bulbous species has been known by a variety of names. The name ''Gladiolus laxus'' was originally published by [[Carl Peter Thunberg|Carl Thunberg]] in 1823. [[Peter Goldblatt]] transferred the species to ''Anomatheca laxa'' in 1971; [[Nicholas Edward Brown|Nicholas Brown]] changed it to ''Lapeirousia laxa'' in 1928; Goldblatt with his colleague [[John Charles Manning]] settled on ''Freesia laxa'' in 1995.<ref name=WCSP_Fl>{{Citation |contribution=Freesia laxa|title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=328131 |accessdate=2012-08-13}}</ref> Separately, in 1830, [[John Lindley]] described ''Anomatheca cruenta'' which [[John Gilbert Baker|John Baker]] transferred to ''Lapeirousia cruenta'' in 1892.<ref name=WCSP_Ac>{{Citation |contribution=Anomatheca cruenta|title=World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=326436 |accessdate=2012-08-13}}</ref> Lindley's plant is now regarded as part of ''Freesia laxa''.<ref name=WCSP_Fl/>

Forms with blue flowers are treated as ''Freesia laxa'' subsp. ''azurea'', other forms being placed in ''Freesia laxa'' subsp. ''laxa''.<ref name=PBS/><ref>{{cite web |title=Freesia laxa - FNA |url=http://beta.floranorthamerica.org/Freesia_laxa |website=beta.floranorthamerica.org |access-date=22 July 2024}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Freesia laxa'' is sufficiently hardy to be grown outdoors in all but the coldest parts of the [[British Isles]].<ref name=Math87/> It requires a light soil and a sunny position. In colder areas, the corms can be lifted and dried off during the winter. It can be propagated by dividing groups of corms or by seed.<ref name=Math87/> It can be somewhat invasive through self-sowing when grown in favourable conditions.<ref name=PBS>{{Citation |title=Freesia |publisher=Pacific Bulb Society |url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/index.php/Freesia |accessdate=2012-08-13 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622234346/http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/index.php/Freesia |archivedate=2012-06-22 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
